function.mechanism: Finely divided metallic particles create a silver/metallic appearance by surface reflectance on external coatings.
common_food_categories: External coating of sugar confectionery for decoration of cakes and pastries (EU food category 05.4)

adi.basis: No ADI established; EFSA (2008) set a TWI of 1 mg/kg bw/week for aluminium from all dietary sources (equivalent to about 0.143 mg/kg bw/day).

efsa.key_finding: EFSA reported that parts of the population, especially some children, could exceed the aluminium TWI from dietary exposure.

adi.basis: ALUMINIUM POWDER (JECFA ID 1756): NO ADI ALLOCATED (1977). Broader aluminium-compound guidance later used PTWI values (e.g., 2 mg/kg bw/week in 2011).

concerns.summary: JECFA's broader aluminium evaluations cite renal and developmental effects as key toxicological endpoints for deriving tolerable intake guidance values.

Rodent oral-exposure studies report gastrointestinal/visceral sensitivity and microbiome-linked effects with some oral aluminium forms, including persistent colorectal hypersensitivity and phase-dependent nanoparticle hepatotoxicity pathways.
A rat oral-exposure nanomaterial study found DNA damage signals in bone marrow for Al2O3 nanomaterials (comet assay) without micronucleus increase.
Regulatory risk frameworks for aluminium compounds include concern for developmental nervous-system effects at higher exposure ranges.

no_concern_confirmed: JECFA ALUMINIUM POWDER (1977) concluded very limited confectionery silvering use and no ADI allocation.
A 2025 Swedish total diet study reported aluminium intake from food did not indicate concern in that sampled population (PMID: 40921320).

adi_exceedance.notes: EFSA (2008) and JECFA (2011, broader aluminium record) indicate tolerable intake exceedance can occur in some child populations when considering aggregate aluminium exposure.

risk_assessment.rationale: E173 itself is authorized only in narrow decorative uses (EU) and historically had no ADI allocated by JECFA for its very limited use, but broader aluminium exposure assessments consistently identify potential exceedance in some child populations and credible toxicological concerns for certain aluminium forms and doses.
key_factors: EU authorization is restricted to external confectionery decoration use (quantum satis in a narrow category)
JECFA additive-specific record for aluminium powder: NO ADI ALLOCATED (1977) due very limited use
EFSA/JECFA broader aluminium guidance values indicate exceedance risk in some populations, especially children
U.S. CFR lists aluminum powder for external drugs/cosmetics, not food color use
